Greenwood Fish Market VivoCity opens on 4 November 2026 at #01-188. Photo: Greenwood Fish Market
Greenwood Fish Market opens its first shopping mall outlet at VivoCity on 4 November 2026, 23 years after the seafood retailer and restaurant started on Greenwood Avenue in Bukit Timah. The Greenwood Fish Market VivoCity bistro sits at #01-188, next to TANGS and Tiong Bahru Bakery, and opens daily from 12pm to 10.30pm.
A bistro, not a third restaurant
VivoCity is the brand’s third address, after Bukit Timah and the Quayside Isle restaurant on Sentosa, which opened in 2015. It is also the first Greenwood Fish Market bistro. Founder David Lee told AsiaOne that half of the bistro menu carries Greenwood signatures, with the other half made up of new tapas, small plates and oshizushi, the pressed sushi. He also told AsiaOne that the outlet is a test bed for global franchising.
The bistro’s own recommendations are oysters, pastas, oshizushi and sharing plates. Alfresco seats are pet friendly, as they are at the two older outlets.
Set lunch and set dinner prices
The VivoCity set lunch runs Monday to Friday, 12pm to 5pm. Screenshot: Greenwood Fish Market, 21 October 2026
The three-course set lunch is S$29.95++ for a starter, a main and coffee or tea, from Monday to Friday, 12pm to 5pm. It does not run on public holidays or their eves. Starters include lobster bisque, assorted sashimi and hand-cut calamari. Mains include snapper fish and chips, prawn aglio, grilled barramundi and an Angus cheeseburger, while steak frites carries a S$12 supplement and pan-seared John Dory a S$10 supplement.
The four-course set dinner is S$45.95++ with a starter, a main, a dessert and a hot drink. Mains include a seafood marinara baked in a paper parcel, John Dory, steak frites and an A5 wagyu hamburg rice bowl. Black cod carries a S$14 supplement and USDA Choice ribeye a S$19 supplement.
Details
Greenwood Fish Market is not halal-certified, though the kitchen prepares dishes free of pork and alcohol when told in advance. Corkage is S$50++ for a bottle of wine and S$80++ for a bottle of spirits, and one bottle is waived for every bottle bought from the menu. VivoCity is linked to HarbourFront MRT station on the North East and Circle lines.
summary: Greenwood Fish Market's first mall outlet opens at VivoCity #01-188 on 4 November, with a S$29.95++ weekday set lunch and a S$45.95++ set dinner.
title: Greenwood Fish Market opens its first mall bistro at VivoCity on 4 November, with a S$29.95++ set lunch

Deepavali is all about light, laughter, and spending time with loved ones, and Bangsar Shopping Centre (BSC) is bringing all three together with a festive celebration this October.
Credit – Bangsar Shopping Centre
Running from 22 Oct to 8 Nov 2026 , the Deepavali Artisan Market brings together handcrafted finds, traditional Indian performances, and plenty of music for a lively outing with family at BSC.
Set up at the Main Concourse on the Ground Floor , the bazaar runs daily from 10am to 10pm , so it’s easy to browse for festive gifts, pick up something special, or simply soak up the atmosphere.
Credit – Bangsar Shopping Centre
There’s more to look forward to beyond shopping, too, with a programme of cultural performances that celebrates the many rhythms and traditions of the Festival of Lights.
Catch the Open- Kacheri Series on 23 & 30 Oct , plus 6 Nov , featuring instrumental-led Kacheri evenings by The KL Conservatory. For a taste of classical Indian dance, Dakhsra Fine Arts will present Bharatanatyam , Odissi , Kathak , and Radha Krishna Dandiya performances on 24 and 31 Oct .
Those who prefer livelier beats can look forward to Dhurandhar Dhol Dhamaka by the Malaysian Bollywood Dance Academy on 25 Oct and 8 Nov , alongside Bollywood and classical fusion, Garba , and dhol performances by The Haven Crew on 1 and 7 Nov .
With music and dance woven into the festivities, even a quick shopping trip could turn into a longer family outing.
Credit – Bangsar Shopping Centre
There’s also a little something to take home. Shoppers who spend RM1,000 at any BSC outlet can redeem an exclusive BSC Glass Dessert Bowl Set , while those who spend RM5,000 can receive 2 sets . Redemptions are available at the Concierge Counter , while stocks last, and terms and conditions apply.
Make a date with the family and head to Bangsar Shopping Centre to explore the artisan market, catch a live performance, and celebrate Deepavali together. Find the festivities at the Main Concourse, Ground Floor, and check the performance schedule before visiting so you don’t miss your favourites.

Want a dessert without too much guilt? Lazy Yoghurt is here to help you with that. Set up at Isetan Scotts on Orchard Road , this popular Korean yoghurt brand will satisfy your dessert cravings. Their pop-up closes on 29 Oct 2026 , so definitely check them out while you can.
Credit – matcha.noms via Instagram
I’ll admit I’m not a huge fan of Greek Yoghurt. It seems a little too close to cottage cheese, and it’s oddly bland. But after seeing how Lazy Yoghurt prepares their yoghurt, I’m definitely curious enough to give it a shot. They even have 4 flavours: plain , matcha chocolate , e arl grey and strawberry .
Credit: matcha.noms via Instagram
Here’s what makes their yoghurt unique: they take a total of 72 hours to be made. Unlike most yoghurts, they allow theirs to ferment for days. This is said to give the yoghurt a tangy, deeper flavour.
Also, they spend more time carefully straining the whey, the liquid that separates when milk curdles. By doing so, the yoghurt is thicker and smoother. Their level of commitment and time spent is kind of ironic, considering their name. Nothing lazy about them.
Credit – matcha.noms via Instagram
What I find most intriguing is their flavours. From what I’ve seen, they have interesting toppings like Honeycomb (S$4) , F igs (S$2) , and Cacao Nibs (S$2) . They also have toppings that originated from Korea, like Yakgwa (S$4) , which is a deep-fried cookie.
Credit: matcha.noms via Instagram
However, if you’re like me and are completely indecisive, you can order their Signature Bowl (S$15.90). As the name implies, you will get fan favourites all in one bowl.
Lazy Yoghurt is located in the Isetan Scotts Basement 1 Supermarket. They’re open from 10am to 9pm , but do note that popular toppings and flavours might be sold out later in the day. They’re only around until 29 Oct 2026 , so check them out!

Suited to anyone after a lighter dessert, though popular toppings may sell out later in the day.

Where can I relax and chill in Singapore?
There are plenty of nature reserves and parks to immerse yourself in nature and chill at. Aside from these, you can also visit the myriad of shopping places in Singapore , or book a private room to relax in.
Is there CCTV in private rooms?
Most private rooms do not have CCTVs. However, some places like Hideout Place do not have locks on their doors so staff can access every room for safety reasons.
1. All In One (BLG)
Best hangout room in Singapore for big parties
The Loft.
Image credit: Bao Ga Liao
If you’ve got a shindig coming up, book a room with All In One (BGL) , formerly known as Bao Ga Liao , which can fit up to 40 of your friends. Amenities are aplenty here: there are board games, a foosball table, a pool table, a portable ping pong table, and darts.
Image credit: @bieeeah via Instagram
MJ addicts can park their butts at the mahjong table as tiles and chips are provided. There’s even a karaoke system with 4 mics so you and your pals can belt your favourite tunes. All In One also provides food and dessert catering, but you’re free to order food from wherever you please. And yes, the consumption of alcohol here is a-okay , except at White Pixies.
Image credit: Bao Ga Liao
Their Loft room is priced at $59/hour which is on the cheaper side for rooms that can host large gatherings. Bao Ga Liao also offers other rooms with different experiences like their smaller White Pixies Studio at $40/hour for cosy gatherings, and the AnyBirdie room priced at $99/hour , which is golf-themed and comes complete with 2 golf simulator bays.
Every booking requires a refundable security deposit between $100-200. Just remember to keep the place clean and don’t damage anything, otherwise you’ll have to say bye-bye to that precious money.
All In One review: “Came here for our class graduation party and for the price we paid, the event room was worth it. The booking procedure was seamless, and it was spacious for 25 guests, with many amenities such as pool, karaoke and mahjong.” – Devin Yan via Google Maps

The haze in Singapore has been raging for the last few weeks, so we’re turning to indoor activities in Singapore to keep ourselves entertained. Before you text your friends to cancel your plans, send this list of activities to your group chats for a solid contingency plan. Have little ones? Our sister site HoneyKids Asia offers a massive list of indoor activities for kids in Singapore !
Fun indoor activities and things to do in Singapore
1. Play laser tag
Gear up for a game of laser tag!
Blast off into an afternoon of fun with this thrilling game. Round up your buddies, pick a place, and call the pros. Laser tag arenas and providers in Singapore will host you for an action-packed experience filled with skill and strategy. Guns out!
2. Relax at jazz clubs
Photography: Yan Krukau via Pexels
Picture this: you’ve got a cocktail in hand, you’re sinking into a plush sofa, and the soothing melody of jazz surrounds you. What a perfect way to end a long week. If that sounds good to you, head to the city’s best jazz clubs and bars for an evening of surround sound.
3. Snap pics at photo studios
Photography: Fotomat via Facebook
Love photoshoots but feel a little camera-shy? Head to photo studios in Singapore to do it yourself. Just grab your partner or a group of friends and capture those memories. Some of the studios even offer cool backdrops and fun props for a stylish shoot.
4. Try a pottery class
Photography: Studio Asobi via Facebook
Get crafty at pottery classes to learn about all things ceramics, from wheel throwing to glazing. Just think about it: you’ll have the freedom to shape and design your own plates, saucers and mugs! The best part? Once your work is all fired up, you can take back your masterpieces to display at home.
5. Hunt down hidden bars
Photography: Mama Diam via Facebook
We’ll happily raise our glasses to the best cocktail bars in Singapore , but when we feel like spicing things up, we look to secret speakeasies for a dash of mystery. Follow us and stroll off the beaten path to find watering holes behind unassuming doors, drinking spots tucked away in shophouses, and other cool hidden bars in Singapore like Cat Bite Club and Ume Maru.
6. (Rock) climb to new heights
Photography: Cottonbro via Pexels
Make like Spider-Man (but remember to hook up your harness) and swing by rock climbing or bouldering spots in Singapore. It’s best done with a group of friends, as you can challenge and cheer each other on!
7. Tuft your own rug
Photography: Danial Zahrin
Always wanted to try tufting ? Get in on the action at studios like Tuft Club and WeTuft to make your own bespoke design. It’ll take a couple of hours to finish your DIY rug, which is perfect for passing the afternoon.
8. Enter virtual reality games
Photography: Virtual Room
Break free from real life and transport yourself into fantasy land at virtual reality arcades in Singapore. All you have to do is put on a headset and you’ll be whisked away to fight zombies, explore alien worlds, hop on extreme train rides and battle dinosaurs.
9. Explore the jewel of Changi
Jewel Changi Airport is a great hangout, rain or shine.
Our airport is known as one of the world’s best for good reason, but Jewel Changi Airport takes things to a whole new level. All kinds of shops and restaurants are at your fingertips – you won’t run out of things to do, for sure. Plus, we can never get enough of gorgeous attractions like the Shiseido Forest Valley and HSBC Rain Vortex. Oh, and the Canopy Park and Manulife Sky Nets will keep you (and your little ones) entertained for the day.
10. Try escape room games
Are you ready to go on an adventure?
Put on your best Houdini impression and find your way out of escape rooms in Singapore – they’re one of our fave indoor activities. Each mystery is a puzzle to unlock, so come with your thinking hats on and bring your buddies to tackle the clues together.
11. Bounce on a trampoline
Photography: Bounce via Facebook
Who says you need to be outdoors to sweat it out? We’ve got awesome trampoline parks including Bounce and Amped . Oh, and let’s not forget Axe Factor , where you can hurl an axe at a target board to vent your stress.
12. Play arcade games
Photography: Cottonbro via Pexels
We’re talking about indoor arcades in Singapore. Fun times await at places like Cow Play Cow Moo and Timezone. Seriously, we can spend hours playing our fave games. Time just flies!
13. Go on a midnight shopping spree
Photography: Ashe Liao
We’re talking about none other than the epic Mustafa Centre . Open till 2am daily, the retail behemoth is stocked with everything you could need (or want). From toys and electronics to apparel and beauty products to groceries and homeware, it’s basically paradise for any shopaholic.
14. Hit the gym
Photography: Sam Moqadam via Unsplash

body:
Brewed by Davine is a home-based cafe in Bukit Batok
Westies looking for an affordable matcha fix: this home-based business needs to be on your radar. Tucked away in a Bukit Batok HDB flat, Brewed by Davine is run by 20-year-old Davine, who serves freshly made matcha drinks straight from her HDB window, with occasional help from her little sister.
With matcha averaging around $7 a cup in Singapore, Davine’s $4.50 Matcha Peng is a steal. She keeps prices low using the oldest trick in the book: old-school kopi peng plastic bags. While most hawkers are transitioning to plastic cups, Brewed by Davine unintentionally keeps the tradition alive, making her matcha affordable and nostalgic.
The localised matcha is under the Peng series. Specifically, the Matcha Peng ($4.50), Milo Sea Salt Peng ($5), and Atas Teh Peng ($5) , which is matcha flavoured with Earl Grey and vanilla. There’s also a Salty Gula Melaka Kopi Peng ($6) , but that is served in a cup.
If you prefer, you can opt for all your drinks to be served in a cup for an extra $0.50.
We were lucky enough to watch her make it from scratch—she started by whisking the matcha powder with some water.
She then filled a bag with milk and poured in the matcha.
The classic Matcha Peng was milky and smooth, with earthy green tea notes that came through nicely. It also had just the right amount of sweetness, making for a well-balanced drink.
The Milo Sea Salt Peng was also milky, but it was a little sweeter and creamier due to the foam. The sea salt was a great addition, cutting through the richness so it didn’t get too jelak .
Davine also recommended her Sibei Chio ($6.50) , which is matcha layered with butterfly pea flower milk and homemade strawberry puree. Sibei Chio is one of her best-sellers. Similar to the rest, this drink was very creamy; however, the puree added a nice strawberry flavour and chunkiness from the fruit.
Her desserts are also loved among regulars, with the Biscoff Banana Shiok ($8) a crowd favourite.
The custard was thick and rich, with a distinct banana flavour. The Biscoff cookie’s cinnamon flavour complemented the banana and made for a great crunchy-on-creamy texture.
As F&B gets increasingly dominated by chain stores and corporations, make sure you also show some love to our local businesses! Don’t worry, the drinks will be well worth it.
For more home-based businesses you can support, check out these best home cafes in Singapore . If you’re considering making your own matcha, here are the best matcha powders to get you started.

Best matcha home cafes in Singapore
With foreign brands making their presence felt across Singapore , there’s all the more reason to support our local businesses. This could mean visiting Singapore’s oldest restaurants for a taste of heritage or eating at beloved hawker centres such as Maxwell Food Centre . For a matcha addict like me, though, it means getting more matcha from my favourite home-based cafes. If you’re a fellow matcha enthusiast, here are 20 matcha home cafes to visit, sorted by region.
18 Oldest Restaurants In Singapore Still Open Today, Including A Teochew Eatery From 1845

State of Mind is a no-frills home cafe in Yishun selling matcha lattes and coffee. Their Ceremonial Matcha Latte (from $5.50) is said to be made with high-quality ceremonial-grade matcha powder, while their Pistachio Matcha Latte (from $6.50) blends rich and buttery pistachio with earthy matcha. If hojicha is more of your thing, get the Hojicha Latte (from $5) , which we found pleasantly nutty and aromatic on our visit.

Tel: 8859 8594

This Home Cafe Has Black Sesame Latte, Ceremonial-Grade Matcha And More In Yishun
2. Horikawa
Image credit: LS Bee via Google Maps
Horikawa is owned and operated by two sisters in Yew Tee, selling matcha and coffee lattes from their windowsill. Their signature drink is the Sea Salt Maple Cloud Matcha Latte (from $6.10) , comprising hand-whisked matcha topped with thick maple-flavoured cold foam and finished with a sprinkle of flaky sea salt. It is said to be a perfect balance between sweet, salty, and umami. Also, look out for seasonal specials; in August, they had the Milo Matcha (from $6.10) : a blend of sweet, creamy Milo and earthy matcha.

If you’re curious about the viral Ya Kun soy milk kopi, but don’t drink coffee, head down to Slow Pour in Woodlands for their Slowya (from $6) : a layer of silky soya beancurd topped with matcha. They also serve Ippodo Ikuyo (from $8) , made with high-quality matcha powder from popular matcha brand Ippodo. Purists can opt for their unsweetened version to taste the matcha’s natural flavour, or less sweet if you need some sugar.

Image credit: @hissorisg
Muslim-owned Hissori is a home cafe in Yishun, its name meaning “quiet” or “calm” in Japanese. For those who aren’t in the North, you can also find them on Grab delivery.
They sell bakes and desserts that complement your drinks beautifully. For something refreshing, their Panna Cotta ($6) , topped with mango , yuzu , or strawberry puree, goes well with the Tokyo Fog (from $7.20) —smooth matcha cold foam sitting on cold-brew Earl Grey tea. A more indulgent combo is their Marshmallow Cold Foam Cloud Matcha (from $7.30) with Brown Butter KitKat Crumble Cookie ($6) , packed with KitKat crumble and milk chocolate chunks.

North-East
5. Brew With Grace
For a cosy home cafe to relax and unwind at, check out Brew With Grace , a Studio Ghibli-themed home cafe in Sengkang that transports you into the world of My Neighbour Totoro . Chill with the cafe’s resident cat, Totoro, and sip on some Yuzu Matcha Oat ($5.50) , made with ceremonial-grade matcha from Uji matcha brand Marukyu Koyamaen, tangy yuzu syrup, and oat milk. To amp up the cosiness, get their Hojicha Apple Cinnamon Oat Milk ($5.50) : apple cinnamon jam combined with nutty, caramelly hojicha, reminiscent of a warm apple pie.
Do take note that bookings must be made in advance through a pre-order form .

Website
Brew With Grace is not halal-certified.
We Found A Studio Ghibli-Themed Sengkang Home Cafe With A Cute Cat Named Totoro
6. Corner Pane
Image credit: Corner Pane via Google Maps
A TikTok-viral ex-canteen vendor runs Corner Pane in Punggol, selling unique matcha drinks and affordable mains. Protein-maxxers should try their Protein Matcha Latte ($6.50) , said to contain 25 grams of protein, while those with a sweet tooth can order the Apple Crumble Matcha ($7) , comprising caramel apple puree and matcha that’s topped with honey foam similar to dalgona and garnished with speculoos biscuit crumbs. If you’re feeling peckish, the fan-favourite Signature Lu Rou Fan ($5.90) , made with tender braised pork belly, mushrooms, and shrimp, is sure to fill you up.

body:
Lazy Yogurt Singapore pop-up has Greek yoghurt bowls
Image credit: @matcha.noms
PSA to all yoghurt fans: Seoul’s Lazy Yogurt is running a two-week pop-up at Isetan Scotts from 16 October to 29 October 2026 , so you have just over a week left to try it.
Image credit: @chubbyyoms
The popular Korean brand, which has locations in Gangnam and Seongsu-dong, is known for their ultra-thick Greek yoghurt. Each batch takes about 72 hours to make, and the whey is strained out slowly until the yoghurt is dense enough to hold its shape in the bowl. Fans who’ve tried it say the texture is closer to cream cheese than to the yoghurt in your fridge. That’s a very different thing from the soft-serve swirls at Korean froyo chain Yoajung .
A First Look At Yoajung: Korean-Famous Frozen Yoghurt Chain Opens In Somerset
A build-your-own bowl starts at $13.90 , which gets you one scoop of yoghurt and three free toppings.
Image credit: @thehungrytara
Toppings include granola, almonds, and fresh fruit such as figs, muscat grapes, and mango. The plain yoghurt is unsweetened and tangy, so the fruit and honey do most of the sweetening. The menu also offers no-added-sugar and fruity bases, including strawberry.
The Korean add-ons are the most interesting part of the menu. There’s Yakgwa ($4) , a chewy, honey-soaked Korean pastry, and Chapsaltteok ($4) , a soft glutinous rice cake filled with red bean. Honeycomb ($4) is also available. You’ll also find Black Sesame (price TBD) and Injeolmi Crumble (price TBD) , made with roasted soybean powder.
Image credit: @d.matcha.diaries
If you’d rather not choose, the Signature Bowl ($15.90) comes with a fixed set of the brand’s popular toppings.
The catch is the price. Add two premium toppings to a base bowl and you’ll pay about $22 , which is a lot for yoghurt. Still, nowhere else in SG serves this style of Greek yoghurt right now, so it’s worth trying once before the pop-up ends.
The pop-up is in the Isetan Scotts supermarket on Basement 1 of Shaw House, a short walk from Orchard MRT Station .
For more cold desserts, our best froyo in Singapore guide covers DIY spots such as Yo-Chi and Yogeek, plus nostalgic picks for OG froyo fans.
Address: 350 Orchard Road, Basement 1, Isetan Scotts Supermarket, Shaw House, Singapore 238868
Opening hours: Daily 10am to 9pm (until 29 October 2026)
Website
Lazy Yogurt is not halal-certified.

body:
1-day Jalan Besar itinerary
Back when I was a student, the cool places to hang out were Haji Lane in Bugis, Tiong Bahru , and Joo Chiat , especially if you loved cafe hopping. Then I started working at Eatbook—our office is located near Jalan Besar—and realised how many solid eating spots in this area were flying under the radar.
Unfortunately, I can’t gatekeep this place any longer, as Time Out has just named it one of Singapore’s coolest neighbourhoods for 2026 , ranking it 20th on its global list.
Jalan Besar means “big road” in Malay, and it started as two swamps by the Rochor and Kallang rivers. Hardware suppliers, auto garages, and lighting wholesalers moved in, and when the area urbanised in the late 1800s, cheap eateries followed to feed the immigrant labourers. Many of those old-school places still stand, now alongside newer cafes, bars and indie shops.
Without further ado, here is my 12-hour Jalan Besar itinerary , featuring a list of tried-and-approved food places for locals and tourists, with a stop at a cat cafe in between. If you’d like to explore more of Singapore after this, our 12-hour Orchard food itinerary is a good next stop.
How To Spend 12 Hours In Orchard: $22.80++ Porridge Buffet, $2 Thrift Stores And More
Breakfast: Sum Dim Sum
Ask any Singaporean where to eat dim sum in Jalan Besar, and most will say Swee Choon. I would too, but you probably don’t need our itinerary to tell you to go—do a quick Google search and most guides will point you there. One lesser-known spot that I think is on par is Sum Dim Sum , just down the road from Swee Choon’s flagship.
Sum Dim Sum has a modern shophouse concept, with two storeys and a mix of indoor and alfresco seating. The menu covers everything from steamed and pan-fried dim sum to baked buns, rice rolls, noodles, porridge, and desserts, plus refillable Chinese teas from $2 , such as Pu Er , Tie Guan Yin , and Chrysanthemum .
A crowd favourite is the Signature Crispy Pork Bun ($6.90+ for three pieces) , which features a distinctive green shade from pandan leaves. You’ll smell the pandan fragrance as soon as it lands on your table. The pastry is crispy and flaky on the outside, and it breaks open to reveal juicy chunks of char siew in a sweet sauce.
I also recommended the Golden Custard Bun ($5.90+ for three pieces) : fluffy steamed buns with a molten salted egg custard centre. For something more filling, the Moonlight Hor Fun ($13.90+) sees silky, wok-charred flat rice noodles topped with a runny egg yolk.
Read our Sum Dim Sum review .
Address: 161 Jalan Besar, Singapore 208876
Opening hours: Mon-Thurs 11:30am to 12am, Fri 11:30am to 2am, Sat 10:30am to 2am, Sun 10:30am to 12am
Website
Sum Dim Sum is not halal-certified.
Sum Dim Sum Review: Beef Noodles And Pandan Crispy Pork Buns That Can Rival Tim Ho Wan’s
Lunch: Jiale Kopitiam
You won’t find a cheaper lunch in the neighbourhood. Jiale Kopitiam , a traditional Singaporean coffeeshop run by the same people as 131 Mookata , has an all-you-can-eat cai fan buffet for just $7 , with no GST or service charge. For the unfamiliar, cai fan, also known as economy rice, is a classic Singaporean meal where you pile a plate with rice or noodles and a selection of toppings such as meats, vegetables, and tofu.
The buffet runs from Monday to Friday, 10am to 2pm, and you get four hours to eat as much as you like. The spread rotates daily, so what’s on offer depends on when you visit. The same coffeeshop also runs a mookata buffet from 12pm for $19.90 if you want to come back for dinner.
For your base, the Yangzhou Fried Rice or springy Ee Fu Noodles make a great canvas for everything else on your plate. I’d typically pile on the Long Bean with Eggplant , Scrambled Egg with Corn , and Lychee Fried Fish , which has soft, tender chunks of fish coated in a sweet-tangy lychee sauce, plus whole lychee pieces for a fruity chew.
Other notable toppings include Honey-Glazed Pork , Masala Chicken , Hotplate Tofu , and Chicken Nuggets .
Read our Jiale Kopitiam review .
Address: 28 Kelantan Road, Singapore 200028
Opening hours: 8:30am to 12am
Website
Jiale Kopitiam is not halal-certified.
We Found A $7 Cai Fan Buffet With Unlimited Lychee Fish, Honey Pork And More
Coffee: Space 23
Jalan Besar’s coffee scene goes back further than you might think. Chye Seng Huat Hardware, a pioneer of Singapore’s third-wave coffee scene, opened here in 2012, and plenty of cafes have followed since. One of them is Space 23 , a relatively new cafe that opened in June 2025, one of my favourite coffee spots in the area.
The cafe has floor-to-ceiling windows by the entrance that let in plenty of natural light, and the tables are generously spaced out, so it never feels cramped even when it’s busy. It’s also work-friendly, with a handful of power points.
…
summary: Here's how to spend 12 hours in Jalan Besar if you're a first-time tourist in Singapore looking for good food in the area.
title: How To Spend 12 Hours In Jalan Besar: $7 Cai Fan Buffet, Cat Cafe And More

Best food spots at JEM
JEM, located right by Jurong East MRT Station , is one of Singapore’s largest malls for Westies. It has everything you need under the sun, including tons of food spots to check out. Here’s our guide to the best food places at JEM to visit when you’re in the area.
1. Casa Vostra
Casa Vostra needs no introduction. The popular Italian restaurant still draws long, snaking queues at its outlets at Raffles City and Tampines Mall , and the branch at JEM is no different. Fresh pasta and pizza are the key items on the menu, with prices kept affordable so everyone can enjoy them .
We liked the classic Mamma’s Aglio e Olio ($15++) ; simple in appearance, the combination of sun-dried tomatoes, garlic, red chilli, fresh parsley, and extra-virgin olive oil made the dish enjoyable, made better with al dente noodles. As for pizzas, consider between the Gamberi ($28++) and Tartufo e Funghi ($30++) , where the former is the restaurant’s signature Newpolitan Red, while the latter is part of the Newpolitan White series.
Read our Casa Vostra review .
Unit number: #01-03
Opening hours: Daily 11:30am to 10pm
Website
Casa Vostra is not halal-certified.
We Visited Casa Vostra Again To See If The Italian Restaurant Fared Better
2. Lau Wang Claypot Delights
Another popular brand is Lau Wang Claypot Delights , where you can enjoy a range of dishes at wallet-friendly prices. The chain is known for its Sesame Oil Chicken (from $7.50++) , served in a claypot and available in both spicy and non-spicy versions.
You must get the Lala Soup ($14.80++) and Sambal Kang Kong ($7.50++) alongside the chicken, as the former adds a rich yet comforting taste to the savoury chicken, while the kang kong is a mildly spicy addition of greens.
Unit number: #04-13/14
Opening hours: Daily 11am to 9:30pm
Website
Lau Wang Claypot Delights is not halal-certified.
3. Warabimochi Kamakura
Warabimochi Kamakura , a famous Japanese warabimochi chain, is at JEM. For the uninitiated, warabimochi differentiates itself from your usual mochi by being made out of bracken starch instead of glutinous rice flour—making it silkier and softer.
Customers seem to love their warabimochi-spiked drinks, including the Strawberry Yoghurt ($9.90/$11.90), Coffee Milk ($6.90/$8.90), and Hojicha ($6.90/$8.90) , among many other options. Alternatively, savour these chewy treats in all their glory in a box on its own. These are available in kinako or matcha flavour, priced at $8.90 or $10.90 respectively for five pieces, and $15.90 or $17.90 respectively for ten pieces . Plus, they also have an outlet-exclusive Mango Yoghurt ($7.90/$9.90) .
Check out our Warabimochi Kamakura feature .
Unit number: #B1-K25
Opening hours: Daily 12pm to 9pm
Website
Warabimochi Kamakura is not halal-certified.
Warabimochi Kamakura To Open In JEM, Get Their Famous Mochi In Jurong
4. Sen Sen Sushi
If there’s one thing Westies have that the rest of us don’t, it’s Sen Sen Sushi , a conveyor-belt sushi restaurant opened by the same crew behind Don Don Donki. That’s right, the popular Japanese supermarket chain has its own restaurant.
A popular item here is the Okinawa Set ($19.80++) , comprising all things seared: fresh salmon, sea bream, scallop, red shrimp, flounder fin, conger eel, tamago and more. If you, like us, can’t get enough tuna, we recommend the Tuna Assorted 4 ($10.80++) . A plate comes with bluefin tuna otoro, chutoro, akami, and tartare. There are plenty of sides to go with your sashimi, of course, such as Edamame ($2.80++) and Lobster Salad ($8.80++) .
Read our Sen Sen Sushi feature .
Unit number: #03-27/29
Opening hours: Daily 11am to 10pm
Tel: 6334 0562
Website
Sen Sen Sushi is not halal-certified.
Don Don Donki Opens Sushi Restaurant In JEM With Wagyu Sushi, Sweet Potato With Ice Cream And More
5. Tsui Wah
Popular Hong Kong eatery Tsui Wah has an outlet at JEM. Established in 1967 in Hong Kong, Tsui Wah is one of the best places to enjoy authentic Hong Kong delicacies. For a sweet breakfast, go for the classic Crispy Bun with Condensed Milk ($4.20++) , which sees two halves of a toasted, buttery bun drenched in a thick and sweet condensed milk, alongside their Iced Milk Tea ($4.30++) .
But if you’re feeling more peckish, the Steamed Rice with Pork Cartilage on Scrambled Egg & Black Truffle Paste ($15.80++) is a great choice, best paired with some Spicy Cucumber ($6.80++) or eight pieces of Spicy Shrimp Dumplings ($10.80++) to quell any heavy flavours.
Unit number: #01-38
Opening hours: Daily 8am to 10pm
Tel: 6978 9271

Tsui Wah is not halal-certified.
6. Eat 3 Bowls
If you take a particular liking towards Taiwanese food , go ahead and add Eat 3 Bowls to your list. The popular Taiwanese eatery has 12 outlets across the country, including one at JEM.

body:
Though I usually skip breakfast , it’s actually the meal I look forward to most. Maybe because I have it so rarely, it feels like a special occasion — almost like how other folks would treat a fancy dinner. After a weekend spent doom-scrolling on my phone, I stumbled upon my next breakfast destination: Warung Kak Yah & PakDin , a roadside gem in Taman Keramat, Ampang .
Credit
I woke up at 7am (a rare occurrence) but didn’t make it there until 11am, thanks to getting lost twice (a not-so-rare occurrence). After what felt like an endless journey down the SUKE highway — aka the road to hell — finally spotting the humble stall felt like finding an oasis in the Sahara.
Warung Kak Yah & PakDin wasn’t too crowded when I arrived, but the heat and humidity hit me hard — I was sweating buckets in no time. The first thing that caught my eye was the local staff expertly flipping roti canai , followed by a tempting spread of nasi lemak and nasi dagang side dishes, all set up in the classic warung buffet style. There were also packs of colourful kueh , perfect for a quick takeaway.
Once I sat down, my orders for roti and drinks were taken right away, but if you’re after nasi lemak or nasi dagang , you’ll need to head up to the front. The service was quick, and within minutes, my dining companion and I were ready to dive in.
What I tried at Warung Kak Yah & PakDin
Fun fact: I discovered this spot thanks to a viral clip of their Roti Sarang Burung Daging/Roti Sarang Burung Special (RM8) , so of course, I had to try it. I was worried the portion might’ve been exaggerated for the camera but to my relief, it was perfectly sized for the price. A low bar, I know, but many vendors don’t even meet that these days!
The dish featured 2 sunny-side-up eggs nestled in crispy roti , drenched in minced meat gravy, and topped with black pepper and chopped celery leaves. It also came with a side of dhal and sambal for dipping.
My first impression? Huge. Even the eggs seemed to be A- or B-sized, which you rarely see at KL stalls nowadays. The beef gravy was nicely runny, simply seasoned with oyster sauce and black pepper. It could be a bit salty on its own, but overall, I enjoyed the flavour.
As for the roti itself, cutting into it was pure joy — it was crispy on the outside and soft on the inside, just as I’d hoped. Paired with the beef and eggs , it was the perfect harmony of flavours that had me excited from the first bite.
Nurul Sate Batang Pinang: Johor breakfast spot in Puchong serving tenderloin satay, kacang pool & outstanding laksa
The dhal and sambal leaned sweet, but I was surprised by how well-seasoned they were. I usually skip dhal because it’s too plain for my taste, but this one was enjoyable. The sambal had a subtle heat — not much, but noticeable compared to the milder dhal .
In the end, I ditched the dips entirely because the Roti Sarang Burung Daging was already perfect on its own!
Extremely pleased, I turned to my partner’s breakfast choice: Nasi Dagang Ikan (RM9) . It came with aromatic rice, fish curry , acar sayur , and sambal belacan .
The rice was fluffy and well-cooked, possibly mixed with a bit of nasi pulut , or sticky rice . I would’ve liked more fenugreek seeds, though! The fish curry, while slightly watery, was well-seasoned with a hint of sweetness I enjoy in nasi dagang . The mackerel tuna ( tongkol ) was perfect — no annoying little bones to deal with.
The crunchy, sour acar timun (pickled cucumber) added a refreshing burst to my palate, while the sambal belacan , though watery, wasn’t spicy at all. But maybe that’s just my high spice tolerance — my partner found it too much to handle (a word of caution for those with sensitive tongues!).
Final thoughts
I’m genuinely thrilled that Warung Kak Yah & PakDin finally broke my recent streak of visiting mediocre food places — it’s a solid 10/10!
The Roti Sarang Burung Daging was everything I could want in a roti canai dish: layers of fluffy, crispy roti , minced beef cooked in a savoury gravy, and perfectly runny egg yolks that spilt into thick, golden streams. It was a beautiful mess of flavours and textures, hitting all the right notes.
As for the Nasi Dagang Ikan , while I’ve had better versions elsewhere, it was still quite good! The aromatic rice and flavorful curry made for a satisfying meal. Honestly, if I lived nearby, I could easily see myself coming back again and again.
People also read:
What to eat at Bukit Jalil?
Where should you go for dinner dates in KL?
summary: Warung Kak Yah & PakDin in Taman Keramat, Ampang, serves classic Malaysian breakfast fare including roti canai, nasi lemak and nasi dagang in a roadside warung setting. The review highlights the Roti Sarang Burung Daging and Nasi Dagang Ikan, making it useful for diners seeking affordable local breakfasts, though the stall can be hot and the sambal belacan may suit spice-tolerant diners better.
title: Warung Kak Yah & PakDin: Keramat’s gem for fluffy roti sarang burung & aromatic nasi dagang

body:
I haven’t travelled the world, because I’m a homebody. Luckily, Shirazi on Dempsey Road let me have a taste of Persian food without boarding a flight. ‘Shirazi’ comes from Shiraz, a city in Iran known for its poetry and art. You can see that same creativity throughout the restaurant’s interior, from the grand chandeliers to the marble tables.
The place felt pristine, more like a museum than a restaurant. Every column features a different piece of art, and I could have admired the decor all day. When I first entered the restaurant, I was hit with the smell of spices, some familiar and some not. Notes of warm turmeric, cumin and many other spices wafted throughout the restaurant.
Mohammad Hosseini , one of the owners and chefs, was heavily involved in the design, as he felt no designer could truly capture the authenticity of Iran. He picked out the art, paint and even the carpet. The murals also add a regal energy throughout the restaurant. Born in Zanjan, Iran, he clearly took great pride in his culture. He also mentioned that he felt a calling towards Singapore.
Do note, my fellow Muslim friends, that Shirazi is not halal-certified and has a bar inside. It does, however, run a Muslim-friendly kitchen that uses halal-certified meat and poultry.
What to order at Shirazi
I’ll only talk about some of the dishes that stood out to me, as we tried so many. I can’t possibly cover every dish, much as I’d love to. While it is a Persian restaurant, you will find inspiration from across the Middle East. Some iconic dishes you may have heard of are prepared slightly differently depending on the region.
Firstly, the Hummus (S$16) was creamy, rich and nutty, with a texture close to smooth peanut butter. I could tell they used fresh chickpeas, as there was none of the grainy texture you sometimes get from the canned ones.
The best part was the pita chips served alongside the Hummus . They were cut from their homemade Pita Bread (S$4.50) , then seasoned with salt and deep-fried. There was a strong taste of garlic, which only made the chips moreish. The chips are very salty on their own, so be sure to dip them in the dips or salads.
Another appetiser I had always wanted to try was the Grilled Halloumi With Zatar (S$20) . Everyone says halloumi squeaks, and they’re right. I could hear it with every bite, and I loved it. The cheese is made with 3 types of milk: cow, sheep and goat. I’m no cheese sommelier, so I couldn’t taste the different milks. It was savoury, rich and well-balanced with the za’atar , and I could have eaten 12 of these.
I also wanted to try the Dolma (S$14) , but honestly, it wasn’t for me. The leaves on the outside were surprisingly delicate, so I barely had to put any effort into my bite. The part I wasn’t a fan of, however, was the filling of rice, herbs and lemon. It was mushy and tasted quite one-note. One of the staff mentioned that in some regions, they serve d olma (S$14) with meat and rice as the filling. Perhaps I would have preferred that.
Zuzu Kebab: True-blue Turkish hawker single-handedly serves amazing kebabs & butter rice in Serangoon
Up next are the mains. I decided to kaypoh a bit and take a look inside the kitchen. I was greeted by fire and smiling faces. The smoky, spiced aroma instantly filled my nose. The vibe was similar to walking around East Coast Park while everyone was barbecuing. The fire was also really cool to see flare up intensely as the fat from the meats rendered. Also, the dishes were prepared by Chef Mohammad Hosseini himself. It was a pleasure to watch a master work on his craft.
Every dish was brilliant in its own way, but the best had to be the Shirazi Grilled Platter (S$120) . For context, I brought a friend who had recently completed a powerlifting meet. For 2 large lads, nothing can be more appealing than a giant platter full of meat.
When the platter of seasoned, smoky and succulent delights arrived, the fragrance alone made our mouths water. Let’s start with a surprising entrant: the Prawn Kebab (S$43 à la carte ) . Marinated with saffron, the prawn had an almost golden hue. It was lightly salted, maintaining the sweetness you can get from tiger prawns. The texture was bouncy and meaty, with no fishiness and none of the acrid taste from the intestine. It was a lovely bite to start.
Another favourite of ours was the Chicken (S$42 à la carte ) , which was incredibly juicy. The yoghurt marinade made it tender, and the spices seeped into the meat. Each bite was as flavourful and succulent as the last. Again, the entire platter was absolutely yummy, but the chicken and prawn were really outstanding.
…
summary: Shirazi is a Persian restaurant at 8 Dempsey Road, with a museum-like interior and a grill menu led by the S$120 Shirazi Grilled Platter. It is not halal-certified and has a bar, but its Muslim-friendly kitchen uses halal-certified meat and poultry. Portions are generous and prices sit on the higher side, making it best suited for groups of friends and family.
title: Shirazi: Traditional Persian kebabs & a 400 BC dessert from a veteran chef

body:
The annual event featuring the best of Japanese pop culture is back! Anime Festival Asia Singapore 2026 (AFASG26) will take place the weekend of 27–29 November 2026 , bringing 3 days of music , entertainment , and fan experiences .
Credit: AFASG26
This year’s AFA is special because it is held in conjunction with SJ60 , which commemorates 60 years of diplomatic relations between Singapore and Japan. As fans come together for a celebration of cultural connections and a shared passion for Japanese pop culture, there is much for them to look forward to!
Credit: AFASG26
Japanese music lovers are in for a treat, as over the 3 nights of AFASG26, there will be concerts featuring acclaimed Japanese music artistes. A special AFA Vocaloid Night featuring Hatsune Miku will also take place on Sunday, the 29th .
Fans of iconic musical duo YOASOBI can also visit a special booth at AFASG26 ahead of their upcoming concert in 2027. For the full concert line-up during the 3 days of AFASG26, click here .
Credit: AFASG26
Another highlight of AFASG26 is the Creators Hub located on the exhibition grounds. More than 100 independent creators will present a marketplace of original artwork, handmade collectables and unique merchandise. You’ll surely find something to bring home as a fan!
Credit: AFASG26
Talking about merchandise, there will also be themed booths by entertainment companies such as Toei Animation , TOHO Animation , Crunchyroll , and more! Look out for exclusive first-drop merchandise from beloved anime titles that will make their debut at AFASG26.

KoHo TAR Hotel in Johor Bahru
Another weekend, another JB getaway. But if you’re getting bored of your usual JB hotels , KoHo TAR Hotel might just make your next staycay across the Causeway a little more interesting. It’s a new budget-friendly boutique hotel with a retro-inspired aesthetic that gives off old-school American diner vibes, a refreshing change from the minimalist, sleek hotel rooms we’re all familiar with.
The best part is that rooms are priced from S$39/night , so it’s an option for anyone looking for a fun and quirky place to spend the night without burning a hole in their wallet.
The current exchange rate is S$1 = ~ RM3.20 as of 20th October 2026.
What is KoHo TAR Hotel?
Image credit: KoHo TAR Hotel
Newly opened in September 2026 , this boutique hotel stands out from the other hotels in the area with its colourful facade.
Look out for playful murals splashed across the building, from a retro orange car and cartoon windows to a milkshake bar design on the 1st floor. Together, they give the hotel a nostalgic vibe reminiscent of 20th-century America, just with a lot more colour.
Image credit: KoHo TAR Hotel
The team behind KoHo TAR Hotel has also shared with us that their goal was to create the 1st themed hotel in JB . Rather than focusing solely on providing an affordable place to sleep, they’re hoping to turn the accommodation itself into something different from your straightforward budget hotel stay.
The reception area is decked out in a wide array of colours and patterns that surprisingly match so well together.
Image credit: KoHo TAR Hotel
It’s a relatively small property, so you won’t find big-hotel amenities like a pool or room service here. Still, the cosy, aesthetic, and affordable rooms make it worth considering for your next JB trip.
What can I expect at KoHo TAR Hotel?
Colourful, fun rooms with basic amenities
Image credit: KoHo TAR Hotel
The retro-inspired interiors don’t stop at the hotel’s reception area. The guest rooms follow the same playful aesthetics, so you can take a step back in time when you retire to your room after a day of exploring JB.
For instance, there’s a blue-and-pink themed room, featuring checkered wallpaper and a bright, bold colour palette for a modern spin on vintage nostalgia.
Image credit: KoHo TAR Hotel
Despite the hotel’s retro aesthetic, you won’t have to worry when it comes to amenities. Rooms come equipped with modern essentials such as air-conditioning , a flat-screen TV , free Wi-Fi , and private bathrooms .
There’s also an electric kettle , toiletries , and a hairdryer listed among the in-room amenities, so you can pack lighter for a quick overnight trip.
Image credit: KoHo TAR Hotel
Previous guests’ reviews have also highlighted the hotel’s spacious rooms and practical features. A guest who stayed in September 2026 mentioned conveniently placed charging sockets, alongside comfortable bedding and powerful air-conditioning.
Many room types for couples, friends & families
Deluxe Single room.
Image credit: Agoda
For those planning to spend the night, KoHo TAR Hotel offers a plethora of room types catering to couples, friends, and families.
Here’s the breakdown of the room types and group sizes they’re suitable for:

Get cheaper rates when you book online
Image credit: KoHo TAR Hotel
Here’s the part that might convince you to make that spontaneous JB staycay trip: staying at KoHo TAR Hotel doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.
According to the hotel, walk-in rates start from RM140/night (~S$43.70) , but booking through online platforms such as Agoda or Booking.com may get you a cheaper rate. At the time of writing, listings on Agoda have advertised stays from S$39 to S$56 per night depending on room type and booking date.
Convenient for a quick overnight getaway
Image credit: Agoda
Another perk of choosing KoHo TAR Hotel for your next trip is its convenient location. The property is approximately 3.5km away from JB Sentral, which means you won’t have to venture far from the Causeway after crossing the border.
But getting to major shopping malls may require a short drive or Grab ride, so factor that into your itinerary.
How to get to KoHo TAR Hotel from Singapore
From Singapore, take cross-border bus 160 , 170X , or 950 to JB Sentral via Woodlands Checkpoint . After clearing immigration at JB CIQ, book a Grab to KoHo TAR Hotel, which typically takes 5-10 minutes depending on traffic.
Those driving up can also head directly to the hotel via the Causeway, but take note that parking spaces may be limited.
Experience a retro-themed stay at KoHo TAR Hotel

body:
Scattering ashes in Singapore
Death, although a macabre topic that we tend to stray away from, is perhaps the only thing that’s certain in our lives – other than the perpetually increasing GST, of course. Jokes aside, having to deal with the remains of our loved ones after they’ve passed on is a process that deserves careful consideration during end-of-life planning.
While you might be familiar with after-death services such as cremation and burial ceremonies, not many know that ash scattering is another option when it comes to honouring our beloved. Should you or a loved one wish to take this symbolic yet pragmatic approach, here’s all you need to know about scattering ashes in Singapore .
Where can I scatter ashes in Singapore?
In case it wasn’t obvious enough, in Singapore, you can’t scatter cremated ashes willy-nilly; in fact, it’s illegal to do so in unauthorised public places, and you might face fines of up to $10,000 for doing so. As such, there are 2 perfectly legal methods to scatter ashes on the Little Red Dot: inland ash scattering and scattering at sea .
Where can I do inland ash scattering?
Image credit: NEA
If you wish to scatter cremated ashes on land, also known as inland ash scattering, there are 2 designated locations in Singapore where you can do so, known as inland ash scattering facilities .
The first one can be found in Choa Chu Kang , in the Garden of Peace . Despite its location, it’s not too ulu ; you can get there via buses no. 405 or 975 and alight at the Nirvana Memorial Gdn bus stop (stop ID: 31121) . The Garden of Peace is just a 6-minute walk from the bus stop.
Image credit: NEA
The second is the Garden of Serenity , which can be found within the Mandai Crematorium and Columbarium Complex in Mandai, and this one’s not too hard to get to either. If you’re not driving there, simply board bus no. 171 from Yishun Bus Interchange and alight at the Mandai Crematorium & Columbarium bus stop (stop ID: 48149) . The garden is right opposite the bus stop and getting there shouldn’t take you more than a minute’s walk.
Image credit: National Environment Agency via Facebook
Opened in 2021 and 2025, respectively, these inland ash scattering facilities are both managed by the National Environment Agency (NEA) . In both gardens, there are spacious, designated lanes for scattering cremated ashes, which can be identified by their pebble-covered surface .
Image credit: NEA
Trees and hedges are also planted in between lanes, providing some much-needed privacy for families and setting a respectful and dignified environment for the solemn process. Speaking of which, the gardens are nicely manicured and well-kept, so feel free to roam the grounds as you see fit.
Image credit: NEA
There are some things to note and guidelines to follow should you wish to conduct inland ash scattering at these facilities, which include:
• Only the cremated ashes of deceased who are Singapore Citizens/Permanent Residents and foreigners whose immediate next-of-kin are Singapore Citizens/Permanent Residents are allowed to be scattered.
• You’ll have to turn cremated bone fragments into fine ashes in powder form before you can scatter them. You can bring cremated bone fragments to the Choa Chu Kang/Mandai Crematorium for this process at least 1 hour before your booked time for scattering.
• Once the inland ash scattering lanes reach maximum capacity due to the accumulation of ashes over time, NEA will periodically transfer ash-infused soil from the scattering lanes at the Garden of Peace and Garden of Serenity to another location within the Garden of Peace.
• Religious ceremonies are not allowed inside the gardens , such as the burning of joss sticks or paper. However, simple rites can be conducted at designated prayer facilities nearby.
• Fresh-cut flowers may be placed at NEA-provided racks, but food offerings and other objects cannot be left behind .
Before you head down to scatter cremated ashes, remember to make a booking via the NEA website by logging in with your Singpass. There is a service fee of $320 , and payment for the booking will need to be made within 30 minutes of selecting your session.
Scattering at sea
Image credit: Heng Lee Boat Services Pte Ltd via Facebook
Also known as a sea burial, scattering ashes at sea is also possible off the coast of Singapore. However, sea scattering is only permitted at a designated location approximately 3.2km east of Raffles Lighthouse , from 7am to 7pm daily . As of writing, the only way to conduct a scattering at sea is by engaging a private boat operator or funeral service provider .
Existing private sea scattering service providers like AfterlifeBro can help charter a boat which seats up to 10 family members from $280 , while others can offer more comprehensive add-ons. For $740 , Unity Casket has a special package which includes religious prayers or ceremonial rites, and even accommodates personalised elements chosen by the family.
…
summary: A symbolic yet pragmatic approach to honouring our beloved.
title: Guide To Scattering Ashes In SG: Do’s & Don’ts, Plus Locations & Services For Inland & Sea Scattering

Using DBS PayLah! in Taiwan
Taiwan is another favourite holiday destination for Singaporeans, because who can resist chionging through Taipei’s night markets or taking a day trip to Jiufen ? If you’re already planning your next trip there, you’ll be glad to know that you can now use DBS PayLah! to scan QR codes and pay merchants in Taiwan , with no additional service fees.
Keep reading to find out how it works.
How can I pay using DBS PayLah! in Taiwan?
Eligible TWQR codes that you can scan using PayLah!.
Image credit: DBS
Pay for your night market snacks and cute souvenirs using PayLah! at over 250,000 participating merchants across Taiwan, covering around two-thirds of the Taiwan QR Code (TWQR) merchant network. That means less cash to carry around and no need to download a separate payment app just for your holiday.
Fun fact: DBS is the 1st Singapore bank to provide this service, connecting its customers to TWQR for fuss-free payments in Taiwan.
Making a payment is easy too, and can be completed in 4 simple steps:
1. Scan the merchant’s QR code
Image credit: DBS
Open your DBS PayLah! app and use its QR scanner to scan the merchant’s QR code at participating stores.
2. Enter the amount
Image credit: DBS
Some QR codes will automatically populate the payment amount, so you can skip the manual entry. If yours doesn’t, key in the amount in TWD before proceeding.
3. Review the transaction before confirming
Image credit: DBS
Next, double-check the payment details. The app will display the amount in TWD , the current exchange rate , and the equivalent amount you’ll pay in SGD . Once everything looks right, tap “Let’s Go” to confirm the payment.
4. Check your payment status
Image credit: DBS
Then check that you’ve completed the transaction ; a payment confirmation page will be displayed once the payment has gone through.
Are there any extra fees?
There are no additional service fees , apart from the currency conversion rate. So if you’d rather skip the hassle of exchanging cash or digging through your wallet for loose change, consider using PayLah! to pay.
Are there any transaction limits?
Image for illustrative purposes only.
Image credit: DBS
Your existing PayLah! wallet limits apply to payments made via TWQR too.
Here’s how much you can spend daily:
• DBS PayLah! – Up to S$2,000 per day
• DBS PayLah! Lite – Up to S$999 per day
BTW, it’s possible to adjust your personal daily transaction limit within the app, as long as it stays within the maximum limit for your wallet type.
Get cashback when you scan to pay overseas using DBS PayLah!
From 16th November 2026 to 31st January 2027 , new users of PayLah!’s overseas QR payment service can enjoy cashback of up to S$3 , with no minimum spend required, when they scan to pay at participating merchants in Taiwan .
The app also supports cross-border QR payments in Malaysia , Thailand , and Indonesia . Spend in these countries during the campaign period, and you’ll get to enjoy the cashback too!
Take note that you must not have used PayLah! for overseas QR payments in the past 12 months to qualify. The cashback is also limited to 1 redemption per customer per month, with only 20,000 redemptions available each month.
Scan & pay using DBS PayLah! on your next trip to Taiwan
Image credit: MuchoTV 무초TV via Google Maps
There’s more to look forward to. PayLah! users will be able to scan to pay at all participating merchants across the TWQR network from 2027, and the bank will also introduce a payment option in Taiwan where major retailers can scan your PayLah! QR code to complete the transaction.
But before that, familiarise yourself with the app before your next Taiwan trip, so you spend less time figuring out how to pay and more time hunting down your next bowl of lu rou fan .

Indian sweets in Singapore are arguably unmatched. We love a good slice of cake or a quick cupcake fix now and then. But there’s nothing like indulging in Indian sweets, and we’re taking Deepavali season in Singapore as our excuse to give in to temptation. With vibrant colours and complex flavours, Indian sweets – or mithai – are synonymous with celebrations and all things positive.
But proceed with caution: these goodies can be really sweet, especially for the uninitiated. Still, we say you haven’t really lived in Singapore until you’ve experienced the real deal in Little India . We keep going back to Moghul Sweet Shop at Little India Arcade and Komala’s Restaurants just a few steps away. But if you’re down for a gourmet twist, hit up Michelin-starred Song of India or Punjab’s Grill for next-level festival boxes. See if you can resist: the sweets that make us feel like kids again are right this way…
Indian sweets for sweet tooths in Singapore
1. Kulfi
Photography: kuldeepnegibombay via Pixabay
Think of this as the Indian equivalent of ice cream, except only milk and sugar are used to make this sweet treat. The ingredients aren’t churned (unlike ice cream), resulting in a denser, creamier texture. Kulfi usually comes in flavours like cardamom and pistachio, though you can also find fruits added to the mix.
Where to get it: Cool down with a stick of kulfi at Banjara Restaurant or Tandoori Corner . If you wanna enjoy it in the comfort of your home, order from Bombay Kulfi .
2. Karanji
Photography: Santhosh Varghese via Shutterstock
Known by a multitude of other names like gujia, somas and pedakiya, this dessert is a flaky pastry filled to the brim with treats. After getting stuffed with shredded coconut, sesame seeds, nuts, raisins, and various spices, the sweet dumpling is deep-fried to crispy perfection. It’s probably one of the most indulgent Indian sweets in Singapore.
Where to get it: Venture into the Deepavali bazaars because we’re sure you’ll find at least one snack stall serving them. We’ve seen Mithai Mandir and Moghul Mahal sell them previously too, so keep an eye out to see if it’ll make a comeback on their menus.
3. Rasgulla
Photography: Divya Jain via Pexels
This syrupy dessert starts with curdling milk, but before you turn away from that mental image, hear us out. Once you separate the chenna (Indian cottage cheese – yup, there’s a whole technique to it), it’s kneaded and rolled into balls. Next, it’s cooked in a sugar syrup, and you’ll get sweet dumplings that are soft and spongy.
Where to get it: You can find rasgulla tinned up and ready to eat from stores like Dashmesh or even at FairPrice . Alternatively, pop by Shamiana Restaurant or The Curry Culture . Both have rasmalai on their menus, which is similar to rasgulla except the cheese dumplings are dipped and served in thickened milk.
4. Jalebi
Photography: Nadir Hashmi
This confection is (almost) sickeningly sweet and sticky. It gets its muruku-like pretzel shape by plopping the fermented batter in a spiral motion into a pool of hot oil. The crisp snack is dunked in a saffron sugar syrup for that iconic orange glow.
Where to get it: We all agree this is best eaten freshly fried. You can get jalebi at Bikanervala or Jaggi’s North Indian Cuisine . It’s an absolute melt-in-the-mouth delight.
5. Adhirasam
Photography: SurianiSuzie via Shutterstock
We call it the Indian doughnut , but trust us, it’s not as sweet as the aforementioned confection. Made from rice flour and jaggery (cane sugar), this treat is deep-fried, so it’s nice and crisp on the outside but pillowy soft on the inside.
Where to get it: Native Special sells adhirasam along with other snacks that you can add to your Deepavali list.
6. Laddoo
That glossy sheen of sugar syrup? It’s gotta be laddoo. Photography: Nicole Nithiyah
The laddoo (or laddu) is the poster child for Indian sweets. If you’re going to a wedding or a religious Indian ceremony in Singapore, you know this will be waiting for you. Plump with ghee, flour and sugar, these sweet treats are made from tiny drops of chickpea flour mix. They’re fried in ghee and soaked in sugar syrup. Sounds easy, but it takes special skill to mould the mixture into those iconic spheres (and you have to do it while it’s hot!). Much respect.
Where to get it: It’s easy to find variations of this sweet just about anywhere, but our pick is Moghul’s Sweets . It’s known for its signature motichoor laddoos, which will complete your Deepavali spread.
7. Palkova
There are only two ingredients in this: milk and sugar. The magic is in the way it’s made. First, the milk simmers till it reaches a paste-like consistency, then sugar is added to the mix. Once it becomes semi-solid, it’s cooled and ready to be devoured. But really, you don’t have to break your back in the kitchen – just pop by Little India to get this ivory white treat.
Where to get it : You can devour this sweet treat by ordering it at Sri Dairy , or find it on Lazada .

Whether you’re dressing up for Halloween , attending a themed party or preparing for an event, finding the right costume can make all the difference. From classic witches and vampires to superheroes, anime characters and other elaborate outfits, Singapore has several costume shops catering to such occasions.
Do note that because many of these stores offer such a plethora of costumes in their inventory, prices vary by age and design. It is best to contact them for further information on exact pricing and details. For you to look and feel good, here are 10 best costume shops in Singapore so you’ll be dressed to the nines.
How I chose these best costume shops in Singapore
These are the 3 main criteria I used to decide which costume store to recommend:
• Variety : The stores on this list offer a large range of costumes.
• Wide price range : From more affordable accessories to full-on costumes, you can pick what best suits your budget.
• Accessibility : I included physical shops, physical shops with online shopping, and an online retailer for your convenience.

1. Costumes ‘N’ Parties
Credit – Costumes ‘N’ Parties
Costumes ‘N’ Parties is Singapore’s largest costume rental and cosplay shop, which means there is a high chance that you can find any costume your heart desires. Located at Havelock II , the store has over 25 years of experience in the costume business. The store offers over 20,000 outfits and accessories , such as wigs across different themes. Some themes you can expect are 1960s – 1970s, Halloween, Christmas, mascot costumes and more. There are even pet costumes for your furry companion to join in the fun.
Credit – Costumes ‘N’ Parties
What I like most is that both individual accessories and complete outfits are available for purchase here. This works especially well when you already have some parts of the costume at home, and just need that cherry on top to finish the look. Alternatively, you can also get a more elaborate, complete outfit if you wish — the possibilities are endless! Besides physical retail and rental, the store also offers online shopping and rental. Do note that prices vary between rental and sale; it’s best to enquire with the store for specific details.

2. Ministry of Costumes
Credit – Ministry of Costumes
The Ministry of Costumes was established in 2016, with the goal of creating an authentic family orientated costume shop in Singapore. The store is tucked away on Henderson Road and boasts 30,000 costumes for all ages and occasions, with both sale and rental options. Be it celebrations, company events or themed parties — you can find what you need here. On the off chance that you don’t, their website states, “ we will go out of our way to source it for you ”, such great service.
Credit – Ministry of Costumes
Some themes you can expect out of their 30,000 outfits are superheroes, pirates and Christmas. There are also masks and props available to further complement your costume. Do note that the store operates by appointment only to provide the most personalised service. The premises are also shared with another costume store. Be sure to contact them before visiting to book an appointment; this also gives you a chance to enquire about prices before committing.

Beverages designed for every kind of drinker, Bar Somma refreshes its menu with Italian-led flavours, savoury cocktails, and addictive bites that keep you reaching for more.
Aperitivo, Savoury, & Renewed Classics
Credit: Bar Somma
Sweet tooth’s cocktail features the electrifying Pine Highball (S$28) with pine soda, Nutty by Nature (S$24) with deep notes of caramel and walnuts from nocino, and Witch Daiquiri (S$22) with sweet hints of floral notes.
Salt, spice, and everything nice (but not too sweet). The Amlfi Gimlet (S$28) infuses celery, Amatriciana (S$26) mixes tomato, and EVOOtini (S$26) seeps kelp, immersing you in a garden of vegetable cocktails, making every sip savoury.
Timeless pours are classic for a reason, and Bar Somma is reminding us with Torino Velvet (S$28) , a creamy coffee-liqueur; Montalcino Cure (S$26) , a unique concoction of rye; II Perugino (S$26) , which contains roasted beetroot and pineapple caramel; and the most intriguing drink on the menu: the Taras Fungorum (S$26) , which weaves mushroom tincture, a concentrated extract of mushroom liquor.
Pass the Plates
Credit: Bar Somma
Plates to pair with your pours start with Marinated Olives (S$8) and Oyster Mushrooms (S$17) paired with beetroot ketchup. These sides go well with II Perugino and Taras Fungorum. The Yellowtail Amberjack Crudo (S$28) is dressed in pine nut milk and pairs well with the Pine Highball. Plates worth passing around are the Angus Steak Tartare (S$28) , Fried Chicken (S$22) with hearty cacciatore sauce, and the Radiatori (S$34) pasta cooked with river crab.
Early Evening Ritual
Credit: Bar Somma
Bar Somma invites you to Golden Hour , happening every Tuesday to Saturda y from 6pm to 7.30pm . You can enjoy a complimentary serving of their Carbonara (U.P. S$22) when you purchase your first cocktail priced between S$22 and S$32 .
Head down with your friends for a good evening with good company. Walk-ins are fully welcome!

Donut fans in Singapore , here’s one to add to your watchlist. I’m Donut?, the Japanese brand known for its fluffy, melt-in-the-mouth creations, is officially opening in Singapore this December at Ion Orchard! While the menu and prices haven’t been announced yet, there’s plenty to know about the brand before it lands here.
I’m Donut? Singapore: Details at a glance
Best for: Donut lovers and fans of Japanese-style pastries
When: Officially opening in December 2026
How much: To be confirmed
Address: I’m Donut? , B2-19, Ion Orchard, 2 Orchard Turn, Singapore 238801
What is I’m Donut?
Photography: I’m Donut? via Instagram
Founded by chef Ryouta Hirako, I’m Donut? was born out of experiments with the dough used in his bakery. The name is a playful nod to the idea that a donut doesn’t have to be what you expect.
Unlike the denser, chewier rings you might be familiar with, these Japanese-style donuts are known for their soft, airy texture. I’m Donut?’s first outlet opened in Tokyo’s Nakameguro neighbourhood, introducing diners to its signature nama donuts.
Since then, the Japanese brand has expanded internationally, with outlets in cities including New York, Taipei, Seoul and Kuala Lumpur.
What to expect at I’m Donut? Singapore
Photography: I’m Donut? via Instagram
The menu is still under wraps, so you’ll have to wait a little longer to see which flavours make the cut. But the brand’s overseas offerings give us a few ideas of what to look out for.
The original nama donut is a natural starting point for anyone keen to try the signature treat in its simplest form. Matcha and chocolate varieties offer more familiar flavour options, while cream-filled versions such as custard and matcha cream are worth keeping an eye out for. I’m Donut? also serves other styles, including glazed and chocolate-coated donuts.
There’s room for a little regional inspiration, too The KL outlet has featured creations inspired by familiar favourites, including Milo, pandan and banana fritter caramel. Whether Singapore will get its own exclusive flavours remains to be seen. But we’re keeping our fingers crossed! Imagine a durian nama donut or one inspired by ondeh-ondeh…
Psst: follow I’m Donut?’s official Instagram account to keep tabs on its opening in Singapore!
Frequently Asked Questions
When and where is I'm Donut? opening in Singapore?
The Japanese donut shop is opening at Ion Orchard this December.
Is this a temporary pop-up or a permanent flagship store?
This is a permanent standalone store, marking the brand's first official brick-and-mortar outlet in Singapore following expansions to New York, Taipei, Seoul and Kuala Lumpur.
What is a nama donut?
Despite the name nama (which means "raw" in Japanese), the dough is fully cooked! It refers to the cloud-like, ultra-moist and springy texture that melts softly in your mouth.
What’s the secret behind the dough?
The unique texture comes from a specialised dough process: brioche base enriched with roasted pumpkin, low-temperature fermentation and handmade creams.
What signature flavours can we expect at the Singapore store?
While the exact local launch menu is under wraps, core global favourites include the original, custard cream, matcha and pistachio & chocolate.
Will there be Singapore-exclusive flavours?
Yes. The Singapore team is expected to unveil local-exclusive flavour collaborations closer to launch.

Causeway Link bus guide
When it comes to planning short weekend trips in JB, flashes of never-ending throngs of stationary cars honking away at one another at the checkpoints often float to mind. However, not all cross-border trips entail wasting hours stuck in a jam.
Other than driving into JB yourself, there are other convenient modes of transport that bring you across the border. Case in point, the swift KTM train . Today, we’re talking about one of the many Singapore to JB bus services , the Causeway Link bus .
Taking the Causeway Link bus is not as complicated as it might seem, even for someone who’s not been to JB in a hot minute like myself. Here’s all you need to know about taking the Causeway Link bus, from boarding locations and fares, to getting back to Singapore after your short respite over at our neighbours.
Quick facts:
• 3 routes from SG to JB via the Causeway
• CW1 from Kranji
• CW2 from Queen Street Bus Terminal
• CW5 from Newton
• One-way fares from $2.60-$4.80
• Cashless payments only (cash payments still accepted for concession fares until further notice)
What is the Causeway Link bus?
The Causeway Link bus, also commonly referred to as CW bus , is a bus service which ferries passengers from Singapore to Johor Bahru, and vice versa. Other than cross-border trips, their trademark yellow buses also operate around a sizable portion of Malaysia, with routes stretching as far as Mersing and Pontian.
For the sake of this article, we’ll only be covering their Singapore to JB routes, but if you’d like to have a peek at their extensive list of routes, head over to the Causeway Link website .
Where do I board the Causeway Link bus?
When you’re travelling from Singapore to the JB customs, there are a total of 3 routes you can take, namely CW1 , CW2 , and CW5 . CW1 buses depart from the bus stop right outside Kranji MRT , CW2 buses depart from Queen Street Bus Terminal in Bugis, and CW5 buses depart from a bus stop near Newton Food Centre , within a parking lot.
What is the schedule and route options for the CW bus to JB?
If you’re wondering about bus timings, here’s a handy table which shows you the first and last bus timings for CW1, CW2, and CW5 – the 3 buses that bring you from Singapore to JB via the Johor-Singapore Causeway at Woodlands Checkpoint .

CW1 buses will come once every 15-30 minutes, while those boarding at Kranji might want to catch their buses on time, as CW5 buses come once every 45 minutes.
As for CW2, it operates 24 hours daily, which means you can board the bus any time you’d like. However, take note that CW2 buses will depart from Queen Street Bus Terminal every 45 minutes from 11pm to 4am, instead of the usual 15-20 minute intervals.
On the other hand, Causewaylink also has 4 buses that ferry you from Singapore to JB via the CIQ 2nd Link at Tuas Checkpoint , if you’re planning to explore that side of the state. Here’s a table which shows you the details regarding these buses:

If you’re travelling via the CIQ 2nd Link, the process for taking a CW bus is the same as going through Woodlands Checkpoint, so there’s no need to worry.
Queen Street Bus Terminal.
We opted to board the CW2 bus to JB at Queen Street Bus Terminal, located between Bugis and Rochor MRT stations, as it was the most centrally located stop. From Bugis MRT, take exit A, and after about an 8-minute walk, you should be able to spot Queen Street Bus Terminal.
Upon reaching Queen Street Bus Terminal, you might realise that there are 2 queues forming. Queue up at the innermost queue as marked by a bright yellow strip of paint; this one’s for passengers taking the CW bus. The other queue is for those taking the Singapore-Johore Express , a different bus service which operates along a similar route.
If you’re a frequent passenger on cross-border buses, you might want to purchase a ManjaLink card from a nearby machine for $10 . It’s essentially an EZ-Link card you can top up with credits and use on CW buses, as well as local bus services in Johor like myBAS Johor Bahru.
You’ll get 50% off your first ride when you pay with a ManjaLink card, along with other benefits you can check out on the ManjaLink website .
Buses for the CW2 route came pretty regularly, and after waiting in the queue for just 5 minutes, we boarded our bus and were well on our way to our next stop: Woodlands Checkpoint . We arrived at Queen Street Bus Terminal at 9.15am on a Tuesday, and as such there wasn’t much of a queue at all.
The queue for the CW bus on a Saturday morning.

Best hotel buffets in Singapore
Buffets in Singapore are aplenty, from seafood buffets to Japanese buffets and many more. If you’re looking for a splurge-worthy option to celebrate a special occasion, we’ve lined up the best hotel buffets in Singapore for you to consider. From free-flow seafood to unlimited pizzas and beers, here are our top picks!
20 Japanese Buffets In Singapore From $18.99++ For Unlimited Sashimi And Yakiniku
1. Princess Terrace
Image credit: Copthorne King’s Hotel Singapore
For a taste of Penang’s finest fare without having to get on a plane, pay a visit to Princess Terrace at Copthorne King’s Hotel Singapore . This heritage buffet has been treating its diners to a mouth-watering selection of Penang’s signature dishes since the 1970s, and is still going strong today.
Watch the chefs in action at the live kitchen, where highlights like the herbal-rich Ark Thui Mee Sua —featuring tender Irish duck drumstick—and wok hei-filled Penang Char Kway Teow are cooked à la minute. Offal lovers will have plenty to write home about with the Too Tor Th’ng , a pig’s stomach soup featuring a zingy peppery broth, while spice fiends should save space for the sour-spicy Signature Penang Laksa.
On weekend dinners, patrons are in for a treat with the luxurious Lobster Hokkien Mee Soup , served piping hot in a rich, seafood-forward broth and topped with half a lobster.
Round off your meal with an array of house-made desserts, including silky beancurd, colourful Nyonya kueh, and crispy-style Ban Chang Kueh perfumed with a velvety durian paste filling.
Prices start at $60++ per adult for weekday buffet lunch , making Princess Terrace’s hotel buffet quite the steal for the sheer variety and quality you get. FYI, families will also appreciate the kid-friendly perk: children aged 5 and below dine free with every paying adult!
Address: 403 Havelock Road, Level 1, Copthorne King’s Hotel Singapore, S ingapore 169632
Opening hours: Daily 6am to 10pm
Tel: 6733 0011
Website
Princess Terrace is not halal-certified.
2. Estate
If you love seafood as much as we do, don’t miss Estate ‘s themed buffets, such as Sunday Social Champagne Brunch and the Grill & Gills Dinner Buffet . Best Tampines hawker food places
We’ve long heard of the debate on which side of Singapore has the best food. To add fuel to this very entertaining fire, we’ve found 25 hidden Tampines hawker food gems to help East-siders prove their point, in addition to these Tampines cafes .
Whether or not the East side is really the best side, we’ll definitely be willing to travel across the island for these delicious Tampines hawker food stalls.
1. Old World Bakuteh & Fried Porridge
If you’re looking for delicious old-school bak kut teh, check out Old World Bakuteh & Fried Porridge , which has an outlet in Tampines. Be sure to order their Teochew-style Pork Ribs Soup ($ 7.50 ) , which features a peppery and porky broth with some succulent ribs. They’re also known for their Mixed Pig’s Organ Fried Porridge ($ 6 ) , a wok hei-laden affair with fresh offal. While you’re here, be sure to try the Large Intestines Braised Mee Sua ($ 6 ) too.
Read our Old World Bakuteh & Fried Porridge review .
Address: 1 Tampines North Drive, #01-34, T-Space, Singapore 528559
Opening hours: Mon-Thurs 9:30am to 8pm, Fri-Sun 9:30am to 8:30pm
Tel: 9819 7696
Website
Old World Bakuteh & Fried Porridge is not halal-certified.
Old World Bakuteh Review: Teochew Bak Kut Teh With Fried Porridge And Dry Mee Sua At Yishun
2. Ho Yun Tim Sum
Ho Yun Tim Sum is run by an ex-hotel chef from Hong Kong, so you know the dim sum here is legit. Here, crowd favourites include the Prawn Chee Cheong Fun ($3.50) , with silky rice rolls encasing juicy prawns, and a thick, comforting bowl of Century Egg Lean Pork Porridge ($3.50) , all priced under $5. You can also get a basket of deep-fried goodies, with three pieces going for $3.50 , including Carrot Cake ($1.20) a nd Fried Spring Roll ($1) .
Read our Ho Yun Tim Sum review !
